system.name: S2Sim
system.one_liner: a selective symbolic-simulation tool that diagnoses and repairs distributed routing configuration errors by checking them against intent-compliant contracts

content.subject: deriving a single-link-failure-tolerant data plane, then simulating it to diagnose B's route-import contract violation

elements.name: S
elements.role: source router with no direct link toward the destination except via A or B; must reach p under any single link failure

elements.name: A
elements.role: router adjacent to S, B, and C; carries two edge-disjoint forwarding paths toward p

elements.name: B
elements.role: router adjacent to S, A, and D; configured to drop routes from D that match prefix p

elements.name: C
elements.role: router adjacent to A and D; carries two edge-disjoint forwarding paths toward p

elements.name: D
elements.role: router that originates prefix p and is adjacent to B and C

elements.name: p
elements.role: the destination prefix every router must be able to reach under any single-link failure

panels.label: (b) selective symbolic simulation

values.what: each node's edge-disjoint forwarding paths in (a) and each node's numbered candidate routes r0-r11 with their guard condition in (b)
values.result_cells: selected/forwarding paths are shown as green arrows in (a) or underlined route lists in (b); the route implicated in the contract violation is coloured red and named in the '(vio) c1: isImported(...)' equation

content.key_idea: Deriving two edge-disjoint paths per router tolerates any single link failure, but simulating the network under B's real deny-p policy shows B's import of [B,D] actually violates that fault-tolerance contract.
content.reading_order: panel (a) first, reading each node's green two-path labels around the S-A-B-C-D graph; then panel (b), reading the same graph's numbered route lists down to the red violation note

summary: This two-panel figure from S2Sim's fault-tolerance section illustrates a five-router example (S, A, B, C, D) that must reach D's prefix p under any single-link failure. Panel (a) shows the derived fault-tolerant data plane: green arrows mark two edge-disjoint forwarding paths per node (e.g. B's [B,D] and [B,A,C,D]), alongside the injected misconfiguration 'D -> B: match p: deny'. Panel (b) simulates the network under that misconfiguration using the paper's numbered-route notation: each node's two selected routes are underlined, and B's imported route r2 [B,D] is coloured red and tagged c1, matching the note '(vio) c1: isImported(B,[B,D],D) == true'. Together the panels show how an intent-compliant design can still be broken by one router's real policy, which the simulation catches and localizes.
summary_zh: 该图分两部分：(a)展示S2Sim为容忍单链路故障推导的容错数据平面，绿色箭头标出每个节点的两条边不相交路径，并给出D对B的match p: deny误配置；(b)用编号路由r0-r11模拟该网络，B导入的r2[B,D]标红并标注c1，对应下方违反的isImported合约。
notes: Added 'comparison' as a secondary group alongside the prior 'evolution': the two panels are also literally the same topology re-annotated to compare a design-time intent (a) against a simulated real-world outcome (b). worked_example corrected from prior False to True, matching sibling Figure 4's identical route-list convention in the same paper: the r0-r11 candidate routes and the violated-contract equation are concrete values the reader checks, not mere annotations. content.relations describes the shared S-A-B-C-D topology common to both panels; panel-specific annotation differences (green paths vs numbered routes) are captured in content.panels.
